observation.visible_scene: A living room with a striped rug on parquet flooring. On the right are a white display cabinet, a wall-mounted TV on a white media unit, and a tall white shelving unit with framed photos; on the left wall hang five framed pictures and a blue exercise ball sits beside a wooden shelf. A girl in a white t-shirt, maroon leggings and pink socks is perched on a large purple exercise ball in the middle of the rug, supporting herself with her hands on the ball and her legs lifted forward.
visible_changes: The girl repeatedly bounces/rocks on the purple ball; her torso and the ball shift up and down between frames, with motion blur on her hair and limbs in several frames (e.g. 4, 6, 14, 17) indicating active movement rather than a still pose.

Over the excerpt the purple ball drifts/rolls to the right across the rug: its center moves from roughly the middle of the frame at the start to noticeably right-of-center near the end, while the background (cabinet, TV, pictures, blue ball) stays fixed, so this is object motion, not camera motion.

The girl's body orientation gradually rotates: she begins in a right-facing profile, then turns through frames 20-30 until by frames 35-41 her back is largely toward the camera, facing the TV, while still seated on the ball.

Her leg posture changes during the bounce: legs are extended forward and lifted in early frames, and appear more tucked or lowered in some mid/late frames (e.g. 15, 26, 36), consistent with the rocking motion.
Her hands remain placed on the top/side of the ball throughout, serving as support.
outside_clip_unknowns: How the girl mounted the ball and what initiated the bouncing are not shown (the clip opens mid-motion).
What happens after the final frame (whether she stops, dismounts, or continues turning) is not visible.
Whether the rightward drift of the ball is intentional or a byproduct of the bounce is not determinable from the frames.
uncertain_details: The exact bounce frequency is hard to pin down because the 15 fps sampling aliases the vertical motion.
The rotation of the girl on the ball and the translation of the ball appear coupled, but the precise cause-and-effect (turning vs. rolling) cannot be confirmed from static frames.
